abstracts.abstract: The proliferation of geo-distributed data stores has fundamentally challenged traditional assumptions underlying distributed transaction protocols. This paper presents a paradigm-shifting analysis of consistency guarantees in asynchronous wide-area networks, introducing the Consistency Decoupling Theorem, which formally proves that the traditional coupling between consistency models and coordination overhead is neither necessary nor optimal for a broad class of distributed database workloads. We demonstrate that by abandoning the monotonic consistency assumption inherited from centralized systems, novel consistency relaxation strategies can achieve asymptotically superior latency-throughput tradeoffs. Our theoretical framework introduces the Concept of Intention Serializability, a novel correctness criterion that decouples the ordering of data operations from the ordering of transaction boundaries. Through rigorous complexity analysis, we establish that deciding whether a distributed execution satisfies intention serializability is achievable in polynomial time under realistic network models, resolving a long-standing open problem in distributed concurrency control theory. Furthermore, we prove tight bounds on the message complexity required to achieve non-blocking coordination in this model. The theoretical contributions of this work reframe the fundamental design space for distributed database systems, enabling a new generation of protocols that systematically exploit workload semantics to reduce coordination overhead while maintaining well-defined correctness guarantees. Evaluation against established benchmarks validates the theoretical predictions and demonstrates the practical applicability of our framework.

Distributed query optimization over fragmented data remains computationally intensive due to the exponential complexity of join ordering in wide-area settings. This paper presents a significantly improved theoretical framework for semi-join based distributed query processing that reduces communication costs beyond what existing methods can achieve. We introduce the concept of Augmented Reducer Coverage, which provides a tighter lower-bound estimation of data reduction potential across distributed sites compared to conventional semi-join reduction techniques. Our analysis proves that by incorporating cross-site filter selectivity correlations into the reducer generation process, the average communication volume can be reduced by a factor asymptotically superior to state-of-the-art algorithms. We develop a novel Integer Programming formulation that captures the joint optimization of reducer placement and join ordering, demonstrating that the resulting problem admits a polynomial-time approximation scheme with provable approximation ratios. Additionally, we establish new complexity results for adaptive query processing under dynamic data distribution, proving that previously published adaptive strategies are suboptimal under burst workloads and proposing corrective mechanisms with bounded performance degradation. The theoretical improvements are validated through extensive analysis across synthetic and real-world query workloads. Our results indicate communication cost reductions of 35-60% compared to established semi-join reordering heuristics while maintaining comparable computational overhead at coordinator sites.

We present Caelum, a novel distributed database architecture that fundamentally reimagines data partitioning for heterogeneous workloads by integrating workload-aware semantic partitioning with decentralized metadata management. Unlike conventional static partitioning schemes that rely on a priori knowledge of access patterns, Caelum employs a continuous self-partitioning mechanism driven by online learning of query affinities. The system introduces the Partition Migration Graph, a dynamic data structure that tracks the evolving boundaries between logical data regions and enables fine-grained, low-overhead partition rebalancing without global coordination. Caelum's core engine executes distributed transactions using a new Consistency-Latency Adaptive protocol that dynamically adjusts synchronization granularity based on real-time contention detection, eliminating the need for static configuration of consistency levels. We describe a prototype implementation supporting both SQL and NoSQL API interfaces, with a distributed catalog implemented as a fault-tolerant Byzantine fault tolerant state machine replicated across data centers. The metadata layer achieves sub-millisecond lookup latency under high query throughput through a novel hierarchical caching strategy exploiting workload temporal locality. Experimental evaluation on a 128-node geo-distributed cluster demonstrates that Caelum achieves up to 3x throughput improvement over conventional static partitioning approaches while maintaining strong consistency guarantees, with particularly pronounced benefits for burst workloads exhibiting rapid access pattern evolution.

We introduce Cascade, a high-performance parallel data management system that substantially improves the throughput and resource efficiency of analytical query processing through a redesigned multi-core query execution engine and enhanced replication management. Cascade addresses the critical inefficiency in existing parallel database systems where intra-operator parallelism is managed statically, leading to suboptimal CPU utilization and memory bandwidth saturation during complex analytical workloads. Our system incorporates a novel Adaptive Parallelism Controller that dynamically reallocates execution threads across query pipeline stages based on real-time monitoring of per-stage backpressure signals, achieving near-optimal load balancing without requiring query-level profiling. We present a redesigned log-structured storage layer with improved write amplification characteristics for Write-Ahead Logging, reducing the synchronization overhead of distributed transaction logging by up to 70% through batched group commit and lock-free log truncation. Cascade's replication subsystem introduces a hierarchical majority protocol that reduces consensus overhead for geo-distributed deployments by distinguishing between intra-datacenter and inter-datacenter message paths, enabling single-datacenter fault tolerance for most operations while preserving cross-datacenter consistency guarantees. Implementation and deployment experiments on a 64-server cluster running the CH-bench benchmark suite demonstrate that Cascade achieves 2.4x improvement in query throughput and 40% reduction in tail latency compared to state-of-the-art parallel database systems, with minimal configuration overhead.
